EMR Camden fire, 2026-03-10 · Modeled smoke tracer & measured PurpleAir PM2.5 over time
Measured PM2.5 (EPA 2024 AQI band)
Circles = PurpleAir (low-cost, 10-min). Diamonds ◆ = AirNow / EPA FRM regulatory (hourly).
● Good (0–9 µg/m³)  ● Moderate (9–35)
● USG (35–55)  ● Unhealthy (55–125)
● Very Unhealthy (125–225)  ● Hazardous (225+)
Modeled tracer (gray cells): NOAA HYSPLIT v5.4.2 with HRRR 3-km met, unit-source emission rate, 30-min averaged output. Cells shown are above 10% of the simulation's peak modeled tracer value (NOAA's convention for ensemble plume displays), unioned across 4 release heights (10, 30, 100, 200 m AGL) as a source-height sensitivity envelope.

Modeled particles (small dark dots): individual HYSPLIT Lagrangian particles from the 30 m release run, dumped hourly. Shade darkens with altitude (light gray < 100 m, darker for higher in the column).
Wind arrow = PHL ASOS surface wind, drawn from the station in the direction the wind is going. Length scales with speed.
How to read this
Gray cells are the modeled smoke transport scenario — relative concentrations from a unit-source HYSPLIT run. They are not measured or estimated µg/m³ and carry no calibration to any specific fire emission rate. Only the shape and direction of the modeled plume are meaningful.

Colored dots are the actual PurpleAir 10-min readings (EPA Barkjohn-corrected) closest to each timestep. Color follows EPA's 2024 PM2.5 AQI band.

Why the model and sensors don't peak at the same moment: the modeled shading is a 30-minute average of column concentration (0–100 m AGL) on 500 m cells, while PurpleAir samples are 10-minute averages at ~3 m above ground. In light, shifting winds (PHL ASOS recorded 140°–240° during the burn), near-source sensor peaks can legitimately occur earlier or later than the modeled column plume passes overhead.

Other caveats: 3-km HRRR meteorology drives the transport — the 500 m display grid is a sampling choice, not a claim of 500 m predictive skill. HYSPLIT places elevated releases at their final height (not along the rising trajectory), and the closest sensor (0.4 mi) is inside NOAA's caution zone for HYSPLIT short-range timing. No dry or wet deposition is modeled — mass remains airborne throughout.
